topics.topic: Authenticated-encryption envelope and key identifier for kept backups
questions: Which authenticated-encryption algorithm, nonce generation, key format, metadata authentication and key-digest algorithm define a valid encrypted backup?
What cryptographic format makes confidentiality and tamper detection—including tampering with release, instant, sequence and key-digest metadata—verifiable?
What cryptographic format makes a kept backup confidential and tamper-detecting, and how is its key identifier computed?

quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
judgement.why: This is the same backup cryptographic-format question already assigned to State 6.

precedent.topic: Cryptographic algorithm, encoding, key handling, and authenticated format for backups
quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
precedent.why: The algorithm, nonce, authenticated envelope, key identifier and cryptographic-version representation are encoding and file-format contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Authentication and CSRF-checking flow for sign-in before an owner session exists
questions: Is sign-in exempt from CSRF checking because no owner session exists yet, or must it have a separate pre-authentication CSRF mechanism?
Is sign-in an exception to A04, or what authentication and check stages does a sign-in request use before an owner session exists?
Is sign-in exempt from CSRF protection, or must Registry create a pre-authentication session or login-specific CSRF value?

quotes: Every operation — read or change, of a service, Kernel or the owner — checks in one order, and the first failure is its answer; a stage that does not apply to it is skipped, and each check an operation states belongs to the stage of its kind: (1) the caller's authentication and its right to the operation (A09) — for the owner, a valid owner session, then for a change its CSRF value (R0-29), then a confirmation value where one is asked (A13);

The owner signs in with the owner credential (R0-30) and receives an owner session (M11), carried by a cookie that scripts cannot read, sent only over HTTPS when the interface is reached from another machine (R0-29), and only to Registry's own origin.
Every change in the owner interface carries the CSRF protection bound to its session (R0-29); one from another session or none is refused.
judgement.divergence: One implementation treats sign-in as an explicit exception that checks only the credential and lockout state; another requires a pre-authentication session and CSRF value or refuses sign-in for lacking an owner session, which the owner notices when attempting to sign in.
judgement.why: The texts require an existing owner session and session-bound CSRF for owner changes but do not state the checks that apply to the request that creates the first session.

topics.topic: Canonical encoding and digest algorithm for confirmation-bound inputs
questions: Which digest algorithm, value encoding, field order and normalization define equality between the shown inputs and the submitted inputs?

How are confirmation-bound values canonically encoded and hashed so every implementation makes the same binding and distinct input tuples cannot become the same byte sequence by ambiguous concatenation?
How are confirmation-bound inputs canonically encoded and digested so that showing and submitting the same values compare identically across implementations?

quotes:
kept as a digest of those values in a fixed order, never
   as the values themselves; a submission's inputs are bound when their digest
   equals it.
judgement.why: This is the same confirmation-input encoding and digest question already assigned to State 6.

precedent.why: The canonical byte encoding, field order, digest algorithm and representation of absent values are encoding and contract details owned by State 6.

questions: Which digest algorithm and exact byte representation identify an uploaded file, and is that identity versioned so later releases reproduce it?
What exact digest identifies the migration file for the mapping, confirmation, closure and audit entry?
What exact digest identifies an import file?

quotes: The mapping names the file by its digest.

What Registry defines is the file it accepts on import; its format belongs to States
5 and 6.
judgement.why: This is the same import-file identity and digest-computation question already assigned to States 5 and 6.

What Registry defines is the file it accepts on import; its format belongs to States 5 and 6.

topics.topic: Exact owner-session cookie attributes, scope, and transport behavior
questions: What exact cookie scope, SameSite policy, Secure behavior, path and treatment of loopback HTTP enforce these requirements?
What exact cookie attributes and request scope enforce the stated browser boundary, including local access and requests to Registry's service-API paths?
What exact cookie attributes and transport behavior must every owner-session cookie use?

quotes: The owner signs in with the owner credential (R0-30) and receives an owner session (M11), carried by a cookie that scripts cannot read, sent only over HTTPS when the interface is reached from another machine (R0-29), and only to Registry's own origin.
judgement.why: This is the same owner-session cookie attributes and request-scope question already assigned to State 6.

precedent.topic: Owner-session cookie attributes and route, host, port, and HTTPS scope
quotes: The owner signs in with the owner credential (R0-30) and receives an owner session (M11), carried by a cookie that scripts cannot read, sent only over HTTPS when the interface is reached from another machine (R0-29), and only to Registry's own origin.
precedent.why: Exact cookie attributes, host/path scope and SameSite transport policy are HTTP contract and encoding details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Scheduling and ordering when daily and post-import backup triggers overlap
questions: If an import-triggered run and the 03:00 run become due together, which runs first, is the other queued, and must both still be produced?
How are the import-triggered run and the ordinary daily run queued, ordered or combined when their triggers overlap?
Is the blocked ordinary run queued for immediately after the active run, skipped until the next start, or retried at another time that day?

quotes:
The import answers once its transaction commits; right after it — or, in
   an owner-only start, at the next start with the tokens (A18 rule 10) —
   Registry makes a backup run outside the daily schedule (A18), so the import
   reaches a checked backup as soon as it can, and the owner interface shows
   when it has (A18 rule 1); a failed run is retried at the next run, and the import stays
   accepted.

The run after an accepted import (A16)
   is made even when the day already has a backup, and keeps both; it is not
   that day's ordinary backup, which is still made at 03:00 or at the next
   start.

Besides it, at most one backup is made per UTC day, the kept backups themselves
   saying which days have one, and runs never overlap.
judgement.divergence: One implementation queues the ordinary run behind an overlapping post-import run and produces both backups; another skips the blocked ordinary trigger until a later start, so the owner notices a different backup count and protection interval.
judgement.why: The texts require distinct non-overlapping runs but do not define how simultaneous or overlapping triggers are ordered or retried while Registry remains running.

topics.topic: Valid secret encodings and byte representation used for length and equality checks
questions: Are length and equality checked on configured text bytes, decoded secret bytes, or a normalized representation, and which encodings are valid?
Exactly which configured representations are valid secrets, and over which byte sequence is the 32-byte length and equality check performed?
What encoding and decoding rules define a secret's bytes, length and equality?

quotes:
A secret — each token, the owner credential and the backup key — is at
   least 32 bytes long; a shorter one fails the start.

A presented secret is compared in constant time; no secret enters a record,
   a log line, an audit entry, a diagnostic or an answer (R0-23, R0-37).
judgement.why: This is the same configured-secret representation, decoding, equality and byte-measurement question already assigned to State 6.

quotes:
A secret — each token, the owner credential and the backup key — is at
   least 32 bytes long; a shorter one fails the start.

A presented secret is compared in constant time; no secret enters a record,
   a log line, an audit entry, a diagnostic or an answer (R0-23, R0-37).
precedent.why: The textual or binary representation, decoding, equality and byte-counting rules for credential fields are encoding and contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Configuration source and namespace subject to unknown-item validation
questions: Which source or namespace is considered Registry configuration for detecting unknown items, rather than unrelated process environment or deployment settings?
Which source and namespace are checked for unknown configuration items, especially when the process environment contains unrelated variables?

quotes:
The configuration holds exactly these items and no other: the store's
   location; the backup location and the backup key (A18); the owner
   credential; one service token for each service of A09 — PresuPro, Client
   Portal, Cabinet, Cabinet Kernel (R0-20, R0-23) — or, for an owner-only
   start, none of the four: Registry then serves the owner interface alone
   and refuses every service call (A18 rule 10).

A missing, malformed or unknown item fails the start; Registry applies no
   default to any item.
judgement.why: The configuration document, namespace and distinction between its fields and unrelated environment variables are schema and encoding contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Mapping lost imported customer references to references minted by a repeated import
questions: After restoring a pre-import backup and repeating the import, how does the owner determine which newly minted Customer must receive each restriction, relationship-end or erasure action recorded against a `customer_ref` minted by the lost import?
How does the owner translate a retention action recorded against a lost import's minted `customer_ref` to the different `customer_ref` minted by the repeated import?

quotes:
What the owner repeats after a restore — erasures,
restrictions, ends of a relationship, the greatest date audit entries were
ever erased by — follows the owner's record of the retention review (R0-60): a
governance document, outside this case (Explicit exclusions), naming each
action by its date, kind and the `customer_ref` or `project_id` it touched —
an audit erasure by its date alone — with no personal value.

The kept export and the import's choices hold
personal data — the import's choices include the names, kinds and tax-id
answers given for the Customers it made, each with the v1 `customer_ref` it
came from: the owner keeps them in the vault,
the owner's Bitwarden that only the owner reaches (R0-23), from the export's
making until their deletion;

A repeated import mints new
`customer_ref`s for the Customers it makes; a consumer that kept one the lost
import minted relinks it in its own service, as R0-79 says for ids
production does not hold.

The owner first starts the restored instance owner-only (A17 rule 1), so
   no service and no agent reaches it, and brings each Customer and project to
   the state the owner's own record of the retention review (R0-60) gives for
   it now — erased, restricted, ended or not — and erases audit entries before
   the greatest date the owner ever erased by, before configuring the tokens and
   starting it again.
judgement.divergence: One recovery procedure correlates lost minted references to newly imported Customers through an unstated mapping and reapplies their restrictions, endings and erasures; another cannot correlate them and leaves the Customers as imported, which the owner and later callers of those Customers notice.
judgement.why: The required recovery behavior depends on translating lost minted customer references, but the retained records described by the texts contain no stated mapping that can perform that translation.

topics.topic: Persisted metadata distinguishing ordinary from post-import backups
questions: How can Registry distinguish an ordinary backup from an import-triggered backup after restart so it knows whether the day's ordinary run is still due?
How can Registry distinguish an ordinary daily backup from a post-import backup when deciding whether that day's ordinary run is still due?

quotes:
The run after an accepted import (A16)
   is made even when the day already has a backup, and keeps both; it is not
   that day's ordinary backup, which is still made at 03:00 or at the next
   start.

Besides it, at most one backup is made per UTC day, the kept backups themselves
   saying which days have one, and runs never overlap.

A backup records, readable without
   its key, its instant, the release that made it, the last audit sequence
   number it holds and a digest of the key it was made with (never the key);
   its age is counted from that instant.
judgement.divergence: One implementation persists an unstated backup-kind marker and still makes the ordinary backup after restart; another treats any backup from that UTC day as the ordinary one and skips it, which the owner notices in the kept backups and recovery coverage.
judgement.why: The texts require kept backups to reveal whether the ordinary daily backup exists but list no persisted fact that distinguishes it from a post-import backup.

topics.topic: Startup validation order, failure reporting, and permitted side effects
questions: When several configuration checks fail, which checks and mutations occur, what diagnostic is returned, and may a failed start leave a newly created store or probe file behind?
In what order are startup checks performed, which filesystem effects may occur before another check fails, and are failures aggregated or fail-fast?

quotes:
Registry checks the configuration when it starts and serves nothing until
   every check passes; a failed check stops the start with a diagnostic that
   names the failed item and never its value (R0-37).

A missing, malformed or unknown item fails the start; Registry applies no
   default to any item.

The backup location must exist and let Registry create
   and remove a file in it; otherwise the start fails.

When the store's
   configured file does not exist and its directory does, Registry makes a new,
   empty store of the running release's version there at the start; otherwise
   the store must open for reading and writing and carry the store
   version of the running release, and a store of another version, or one
   that does not open, fails the start — bringing a store to a new version is
   a step of the release, not of the start.
judgement.divergence: One implementation validates all non-mutating checks first and leaves no store or probe artifact when a later check fails; another creates the empty store or probe file before discovering another failure, and implementations may report either the first failure or all failures, which the owner notices in diagnostics and filesystem state.
judgement.why: The startup rules require checks and filesystem mutations but leave their precedence, failure aggregation and cleanup behavior open.
